title: refactor(gateway): extract source-agnostic desktop relay core
body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Gateway's remote-desktop observer is hardwired to cloud-worker environments: the observer lifecycle, token minting, WebSocket relay, and view-only enforcement all live inside `src/gateway/worker-environments/` and assume an SSH-forwarded unix socket. Upcoming work adds more desktop sources (the Gateway host's own screen, paired nodes), which need the same relay pipeline without the worker coupling.

## Why This Change Was Made

Pure extraction refactor, zero behavior change: the source-agnostic core moves to `src/gateway/desktop/` — an `RfbAttachment` union (unix socket | loopback TCP), a generic desktop session registry (8-observer cap, single controller with `control-taken` eviction, 60s linger, owner-epoch fencing, typed stale-owner/stopped errors), the observe-token + WS relay bridge, and the RFB view-only filter. `desktop-tunnel.ts` keeps only worker-specific SSH acquisition and app launch, plugged into the shared registry as start/teardown hooks; its external API is unchanged. The observe WS path moves from `/worker-desktop/observe` to `/desktop/observe` — private contract, clients consume `wsPath` verbatim from the `worker.desktop.observe` RPC result. Also drops a `now()` option that was dead code before the refactor.

## User Impact

No user-visible change. Cloud-worker desktop observers (Labs `cloudWorkers.desktop`) behave identically: same RPC surface, same token format and TTL, same observer semantics, same view-only enforcement. This unblocks follow-up PRs that add a Gateway-host desktop source and node desktop streaming.

## Evidence

- P1 race fix: the shared registry's `stopSuperseded()` now fences only strictly older owner epochs, preserving a same-epoch observe session when app launch claimed the epoch first.
- Regression coverage: `desktop-tunnel.test.ts` reproduces the launch/observe ordering and proves the same-epoch desktop session remains alive.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/desktop src/gateway/worker-environments`: 177 files, 2,013 tests passed on head `57bc9790217`, including the new P1 regression.
- `node --import tsx scripts/check-deadcode-exports.mts`: production, full-tree, and script scans passed with 0 entries.
- Exact-head CI run `31570657246`: green.
- Codex autoreview over the rebased full bundle: no accepted/actionable findings.
- `git diff --check` clean.

title: feat(webui): auto-request notification permission on first chat send
body:
## What Problem This Solves

Enabling Control UI notifications is manual-only today (Settings -> Notifications), so most operators never turn them on and miss agent completions.

## Why This Change Was Made

Requested by maintainer: auto-ask once on the first real prompt send, never re-ask after denial; Settings already surfaces the denied/blocked state as the manual repair path. The one-shot flag lives in per-origin `localStorage` because notification permission itself is per-browser/per-origin state. The browser permission call fires synchronously during an actively dispatching, direct, non-command composer gesture; subscription and Gateway registration continue asynchronously after permission is granted. Deferred catalog handoffs, Skill Workshop sends, widgets, and recognized commands cannot consume the one-shot. In the macOS app the same hook routes to the native permission prompt only while permission is `notDetermined`, and never auto-opens System Settings after denial.

## User Impact

The first real chat prompt in a supported, connected browser triggers the browser permission prompt; accepting registers the web push subscription immediately. Denying or dismissing means the browser is never auto-asked again; Settings -> Notifications continues to show status and blocked hints and remains the manual path. No new settings or configuration surface is added.

## Evidence

- ClawSweeper-requested paired proof: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/app/notifications-auto-prompt.test.ts ui/src/pages/chat/chat-pane-retained-presentation.test.ts` passed both shards: notification policy 18/18 (976ms) and retained-presentation handoff 7/7 (7.55s). Coverage proves the gesture fact is present during synchronous browser event dispatch and absent in the queued microtask, alongside permission, dismissal, direct composer, programmatic, command, disconnected, and empty-send cases.
- `pnpm docs:list` passed and indexed `web/notifications.md`.
- Local `node scripts/check-changed.mjs`: conflict-marker check passed, but the max-lines ratchet raced an advancing `origin/main` and requested removal of baseline entries for `extensions/discord/src/voice/manager.e2e.test.ts`, `extensions/discord/src/voice/manager.ts`, `extensions/discord/src/voice/realtime.ts`, `extensions/openai/realtime-voice-provider.test.ts`, and `extensions/openai/realtime-voice-provider.ts`, all untouched by this PR. Remote Crabbox/Testbox backends were unavailable on this host (`no ready provider for workload=ci-fast`; provider doctors failed/timed out), so the wrapper used its authorized local fallback. Hosted exact-head CI is the authoritative proof for this known stale-origin race and remains mandatory before landing.
- Fresh Codex autoreview (`gpt-5.6-sol`, high) after each ClawSweeper correction was clean with 0 accepted/actionable findings.
- ClawSweeper findings addressed: programmatic and deferred sends cannot consume the one-shot, browser permission is requested synchronously before deferred subscription work, and the documentation identifies Settings as the management and recovery path.
- The prompt itself is browser chrome rather than page UI, so before/after screenshots do not apply. The post-permission subscription flow remains the same shipped `webPush.enable()` path used by the Settings button.

Fixes #122411

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where sandboxed agents receiving DOCX and other unsupported document attachments were told that the format was unsupported even after OpenClaw had copied the file into their workspace.

## Why This Change Was Made

Document self-service now happens after inbound media staging. Sandboxed turns receive only the successful `media/inbound/...` path for each attachment; failed or partial staging keeps the existing unsupported-format message. Non-sandbox policy remains unchanged.

The canonical staged media facts cover both local staging and remote pre-understanding staging. No host path, broad mount, fallback reader, or compatibility path was added.

## User Impact

Sandboxed agents can use their existing read and shell tools on staged document attachments instead of dead-ending on an unsupported-format notice.

title: fix(device-pair): log bootstrap token revoke and QR temp cleanup failures
body:
<!--
Related: gap finding device-pair-revoke-silent-failure
-->

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators using `/pair qr` would have bootstrap token revocation failures silently swallowed when QR delivery or rendering fails and the command falls back to a setup code. If `revokeDeviceBootstrapToken` failed, the old single-use bootstrap token remained valid until expiration with no recorded diagnostic.

## Why This Change Was Made

The QR fallback paths in `extensions/device-pair/index.ts` treated bootstrap token revocation and temporary QR directory cleanup as best-effort operations, but used empty `.catch(() => {})` handlers that hid failures from operators and logs. This change records a `warn` log for both failure modes so the issue is observable without blocking the setup-code fallback. Two regression tests verify the warning is emitted when revocation fails after QR delivery failure and after webchat QR render failure.

## User Impact

Operators and developers can now see in logs when a bootstrap token revocation or QR temp cleanup failed during `/pair qr` fallback, making it possible to detect and respond to stuck security state instead of relying on the 10-minute token TTL to eventually expire the token.

## Evidence

### Tests

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/device-pair/index.test.ts
```

Result: **67 passed** (2 new regression tests for revocation-failure logging).

### Type check

```bash
pnpm check:test-types
```

Result: passed.

### Lint

```bash
node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.core.json extensions/device-pair/index.ts extensions/device-pair/index.test.ts
```

Result: 0 warnings, 0 errors.

### Before fix

`extensions/device-pair/index.ts:895`, `:921`, and `:910` contained empty `.catch(() => {})` handlers:

```ts
await revokeDeviceBootstrapToken({ token: payload.bootstrapToken }).catch(() => {});
await rm(path.dirname(qrFilePath), { recursive: true, force: true }).catch(() => {});
```

A failed revocation produced no log output.

### After fix

Failed revocation and cleanup now emit structured warnings:

```ts
await revokeDeviceBootstrapToken({ token: payload.bootstrapToken }).catch(
  (revokeErr: unknown) => {
    api.logger.warn?.(
      `device-pair: failed to revoke bootstrap token (${String(revokeErr)})`,
    );
  },
);
```

Proved this change at exact heads using a secretless GitHub Actions workflow that runs both an injected-runtime test and a boundary test (real plugin SDK channel runtime + real bootstrap-token state operations) against `main` (before) and the PR head (after). title: feat(gateway): add /startupz startup probe and fix deployment template admission
body:
## What Problem This Solves

Orchestrators (Kubernetes, Fly, Render, container platforms) have no probe that answers "has the Gateway finished starting?" without also folding in downstream channel health. `/readyz` flips to 503 when any channel account hard-fails (`blocked`, `terminal-disconnect`, post-grace `not-running` — `src/gateway/server/readiness.ts`), so one broken Telegram account takes an otherwise healthy Gateway and Control UI out of traffic rotation or blocks a rollout. There is also no HTTP surface exposing the running version, which makes "which build is this deployment actually running?" needlessly hard to answer for cloud operators.

The bundled deployment templates compound this:

- `fly.toml` declared no health checks at all.
- `render.yaml` used `/health` (pure liveness) as Render's traffic-admission signal.
- The Kubernetes manifest combined the mutable `:slim` tag with `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent` (upgrades silently never happen) and an init container that unconditionally overwrote the persisted `openclaw.json` and workspace `AGENTS.md` on every pod start, erasing product-made edits.
- `docs/install/fly.md` still claimed the image `HEALTHCHECK` is pinned to port 18789; stale since `bc4221a07e9` (#116639) made `docker-healthcheck` resolve the active Gateway lock port.

## Why This Change Was Made

First step of the cloud-container deployment track: give every host one correct, additive probe contract before building anything platform-specific. `/readyz` semantics are a shipped public contract (existing manifests probe it), so this adds a probe rather than changing one.

- New `/startup` + `/startupz` routes: `200 {"ok":true,"status":"started"}` once startup work is complete and the Gateway is not draining; `503` with `status:"starting"` (plus `pendingReason` for privileged callers) during startup; `503` with `status:"draining"` during drain. Channel health is never consulted.
- The startup policy is one factory (`createStartupChecker`); the readiness checker now composes it instead of duplicating the startup/draining branches.
- Version (`resolveRuntimeServiceVersion`) and `uptimeMs` are included only for local-direct or authenticated callers, reusing the exact detail-gating already applied to `/readyz` subsystem names (now a shared helper). Remote unauthenticated probes get `{ok,status}` only — no build fingerprinting surface.
- Templates now use `/startupz` for startup/traffic admission, keep `/healthz` for liveness, and leave `/readyz` for channel-aware monitoring. K8s image pinned to the immutable `2026.7.1-2-slim` tag; init container seeds config only when missing.

## User Impact

- A failed channel account no longer evicts a healthy Gateway/Control UI from Service endpoints or fails platform health checks on the bundled templates.
- Operators and supervisors can read the running Gateway version over HTTP with their existing token (or locally) — no WebSocket handshake needed.
- Kubernetes deployments stop silently ignoring upgrades and stop losing config edits on pod restart.
- No behavior change to `/healthz`, `/readyz`, or any existing response shape. No new config or env surface.

## Evidence

- Regression proof: the new assertions fail on pre-change code (`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server-http.probe.test.ts src/gateway/server.plugin-http-auth.test.ts` → 6 failed pre-fix, all for the missing routes/factory).
- Post-fix: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server-http.probe.test.ts src/gateway/server.plugin-http-auth.test.ts src/gateway/server/readiness.test.ts` green (output in PR checks / see below).
- New coverage: startup lifecycle transitions (starting → started → draining), hard channel failure flips `/readyz` but not `/startupz`, detail gating (remote unauthenticated gets minimal body; authenticated gets version/uptime/pendingReason), GET/HEAD parity with Content-Length, 404 on suffixed probe paths.
- K8s image tag verified against Docker Hub's exact-tag API (active amd64/arm64 manifest) and the `<release-tag>-slim` publication rule in `.github/workflows/docker-release.yml`.
- Docs updated: `docs/gateway/health.md` (probe table + semantics), `docs/install/{docker,fly,kubernetes,render}` including the corrected Fly healthcheck-port explanation.

title: fix(feishu): group chats keep the old agent config after a hot reload
body:
Related: #111570

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators who edit an agent's configuration while the gateway is running would keep getting the old configuration on every Feishu **group** message, while the same edit takes effect immediately in DMs and on the CLI.

Editing `agents.entries[*]` (model, tools, and anything else the agent turn reads) is a hot reload: the gateway applies it and logs `config hot reload applied`. A Feishu DM sent right after picks up the change. A Feishu group message does not: it keeps running against the configuration captured when the channel account started, until the gateway or channel is restarted.

A stale `tools.allow` surfaces loudly as `No callable tools remain after resolving explicit tool allowlist`.

**Correction (2026-08-12):** an earlier revision of this description also claimed a stale `model.primary` keeps serving the previous model, citing the second reporter on #111570. **I have since disproved that for current main**: see the gateway-boundary probe below. Model selection does not flow through the handler's config on this path, so it is unaffected by this change. The claim was wrong and is withdrawn.

Because the CLI runs in a fresh process and reads current config, the natural way to verify a fix ("run `openclaw agent …` and see if it works now") reports success while every inbound group turn keeps using the old config.

## Why This Change Was Made

`handleFeishuMessage` received the configuration captured at account start (`startAccount` → `monitorFeishuProvider` → `monitorSingleAccount` → the handler, with no refresh anywhere in that chain) and only re-read the live snapshot inside an `if (isDirect)` branch. Everything a group turn resolves from that object (account resolution, group admission, model, tool policy) therefore came from the startup config.

The fix gives the whole turn one config identity at the entry point, so account resolution, admission, model, and tool policy all read the same live snapshot. This is the shape Telegram adopted in #103510 for the identical problem. It also means admission checks now run against current config rather than startup config, which is stricter than before, not looser.

That made the `if (isDirect)` refresh branch dead: `runtime.config.current()` is reference-stable (`src/plugins/runtime/runtime-config.ts:11` returns `getRuntimeConfig`, asserted in `runtime-config.test.ts:31`), so its `currentCfg !== effectiveCfg` guard can no longer be true. It is removed in the same change. Net production delta is **−10 lines**.

One deliberate deviation to flag for review: `src/plugins/runtime/types-core.ts:310` documents "Prefer config passed into the active call path." Here the passed config *is* the stale value, which is why #103510 made the same deviation for Telegram.

Not addressed here, recorded as follow-up: other channel adapters may carry account-start config into turns the same way, which is the audit @obviyus asked for on #111570. Also untouched: the broadcast adapter at `extensions/feishu/src/bot.ts` builds its turn from `cfg` rather than `effectiveCfg`; with this change both are live, but the asymmetry remains worth a separate look.

## User Impact

Editing an agent's model, tool policy, or other `agents.entries` settings now takes effect on the next Feishu group message, the same as it already did for DMs and the CLI. No restart, no new configuration, and no operator action required. Behavior for DMs, and for anyone not editing config at runtime, is unchanged.

## Evidence

Added a table-driven regression in `extensions/feishu/src/bot.test.ts` covering both chat types. It supplies an account-start config carrying `agents.list[0].model.primary = "startup-model"` and a live runtime config carrying `"live-model"`, dispatches one inbound message, and asserts which config reached agent dispatch.

The DM case is the control: it passes both before and after, which is what makes the group result meaningful: the harness can demonstrably observe a fresh config, so the group failure is a property of production code and not of the test.

**Before**: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/feishu/src/bot.test.ts`, exit 1:

```
     × dispatches group turns with the live runtime config 11ms
AssertionError: expected 'startup-model' to be 'live-model' // Object.is equality
 Test Files  1 failed (1)
      Tests  1 failed | 101 passed (102)
```

**After**: same command, exit 0:

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  102 passed (102)
```

**No regression**: `pnpm test:extension feishu`, run against a stashed baseline and against this change:

| | total | passed | failed |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| baseline (change stashed) | 1575 | 1574 | 1 |
| this change | 1577 | 1576 | 1 |

The one remaining failure is identical in both runs: `reply-dispatcher.test.ts > createFeishuReplyDispatcher streaming behavior > shows raw command detail in streaming card tool status`, already red on `main` at `fa03d9b913` and untouched here, so per `CONTRIBUTING.md` it is not addressed in this PR.

`oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` on both changed files: exit 0.

One intermediate result worth reporting: a first attempt omitted the optional chain on `config?.current()` and broke 16 tests in `bot.broadcast.test.ts` (`TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'current')`), because several runtime doubles have no `config` slot and the previous DM-only call site never exercised them. The focused test file was green at that point; only the wider lane caught it.

### Real-config proof (added after ClawSweeper review)

The evidence above was mocked end to end: `config.current` was a stub returning a literal, so it never exercised the production config path. Added `inbound runtime config freshness (real config file)`, which writes the hot-reloaded config to a **real file**, points the Feishu runtime at the production `getRuntimeConfig({ skipPluginValidation: true, pin: false })`, and asserts the group turn dispatches with the on-disk config. Only the Feishu transport and agent dispatch remain stubbed; the config plumbing under test is production.

That immediately surfaced something the stub had hidden: the real loader normalizes the legacy `agents.list` roster into keyed `agents.entries`. The stubbed config returned whatever literal the test wrote, so this transformation never ran. The assertion now reads both shapes, so it is about config identity rather than roster shape.

Red/green for that case, against the same command:

```
     × a group turn reads the hot-reloaded config file, not the account-start snapshot 14ms
     × dispatches group turns with the live runtime config 3ms
AssertionError: expected 'startup-model' to be 'live-model' // Object.is equality
      Tests  2 failed | 101 passed (103)      exit 1
```
```
      Tests  103 passed (103)                 exit 0
```
Red was produced by checking out the pre-fix `bot.ts` from the parent commit, not by stashing. The fix is committed, so a working-tree stash was a no-op and initially produced a false green. Worth stating because that false green would have made the whole proof meaningless.

Full lane after the addition: `pnpm test:extension feishu` → 1578 total, 1577 passed, 1 failed, the same pre-existing `reply-dispatcher.test.ts` failure as the stashed baseline. `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` on the changed test: exit 0.

### What could not be produced, and why

A live-Feishu or mock-transport proof is not available to me here, and I would rather say so than imply otherwise:

- There is no mock Feishu transport in this repo. `extensions/qa-lab/src/live-transports/` covers `discord`, `matrix`, `slack`, `telegram`, `whatsapp`, but no `feishu`, and those adapters are **live** transports backed by `credential-lease.runtime.ts`, not mocks.
- A live proof therefore needs a real Feishu app, tenant, and group, which I do not have.

The nearest accepted precedent I could find for an external contributor on this channel is #103513, which ran the real production function against a local HTTP server standing in for the Feishu API and was rated `proof: sufficient`. The proof above follows the same principle, real production code path, stand-in only at the external boundary, applied at the turn-entry boundary this change touches.

**A gateway-boundary probe is achievable, and here is the design.** After the second review I checked whether real Feishu ingress can be driven locally. It can, without credentials or network:

- `monitorWebhook` opens **its own HTTP server** (`extensions/feishu/src/monitor.transport.ts:385`) on `webhookHost`:`webhookPort`, serving `webhookPath` (default `/feishu/events`).
- Webhook mode requires only `verificationToken` and `encryptKey` (`monitor.account.ts:519-523`); both can be arbitrary local values, and no outbound Feishu call occurs on that startup path.
- Request auth is `sha256(timestamp + nonce + encryptKey + rawBody)` in `x-lark-signature` (`monitor.transport.ts:113-116`), reproducible locally.
- The body is parsed as **plain JSON** (`parseFeishuWebhookPayload`, `monitor.transport.ts:84-91`); no AES envelope is needed, and dispatch runs with `needCheck: false`.
- From there it is the production path: `buildFeishuWebhookEnvelope` → `eventDispatcher.invoke(...)` → `handleFeishuMessage` → turn.

So a probe can boot a gateway with Feishu in webhook mode plus a mock provider, POST a signed group message, hot-reload the config, POST again, and observe **which model the provider is actually asked for** across the two turns. That is exactly the "hot-reloaded gateway completing an inbound group turn" the review asks for.

### I built that probe. Here is what it showed, including what it disproved.

The probe boots a real gateway with Feishu active in webhook mode, POSTs a **signed** group message to the plugin's own ingress, hot-reloads config on disk, POSTs a second message, and records what the agent turn asks the provider for. The ingress half works exactly as designed:

```
[feishu] starting feishu[default] (mode: webhook)
[feishu] Webhook server listening on 127.0.0.1:50899
[probe] signed webhook POST probe-msg-1 -> HTTP 200
[feishu] feishu[default]: received message from ou_probe_sender in oc_probe_group (group)
[feishu] feishu[default]: group session scope=group, peer=oc_probe_group
[reload] config change detected; evaluating reload (agents.defaults.model.primary)
[reload] config hot reload applied (agents.defaults.model.primary)
```

So signed ingress, group admission, a completed agent turn, and a real gateway hot reload all reproduce locally with throwaway credentials.

**Then it disproved part of my own claim.** Using `agents.defaults.model.primary` as the observable, both branches produce the same result:

| build | models the provider was asked for |
|---|---|
| with this fix | `["probe-startup-model", "probe-live-model"]` |
| pre-fix `bot.ts` (parent commit) | `["probe-startup-model", "probe-live-model"]` |

Identical. The reload applied in both runs and the fix was verifiably absent in the second, so **model selection does not travel through the handler's config here** and this change does not affect it. That is why the model claim above is withdrawn. Running the red case is the only reason I did not submit a probe that discriminates nothing.

**Then I worked out exactly which config path this change can affect, by elimination.** Four observables, each run red/green against the same probe:

| observable | outcome | why |
|---|---|---|
| `agents.defaults.model.primary` | does not discriminate | resolved by core from the live snapshot, not from the handler's config |
| top-level `tools.allow` | does not discriminate | global policy, also resolved from the live snapshot |
| `agents.defaults.tools` | not a config key | `agents.defaults: Unrecognized key: "tools"` |
| **`agents.entries.<id>.tools`** | **cannot be exercised in this harness** | see below |

The last row is the one that matters, because it is exactly what #111570 reports: the reporter's error reads `agents.main.tools.allow: message`. And it is the one path an ephemeral gateway structurally cannot reload:

```
[reload] config change detected; evaluating reload (agents.entries.main.tools)
[reload] config reload failed: GatewayReloadRequiresRecoveryOwnerError: config reload requires a managed gateway restart owner for irreversible hot reload
```

`shouldRefreshContextWindowCache` returns true for every path starting with `agents.entries.` (`src/gateway/config-reload-recovery.ts:98-108`), which makes the plan recovery-requiring; `assertIrreversibleReloadPlanHasRecoveryOwner` then throws unless `restartRecoveryAvailable`, which is `params.requestRecoveryRestart !== undefined` (`src/gateway/server-reload-managed.ts:62-63`). That emitter comes from a supervising service. The #111570 reporter ran a launchd-managed gateway and therefore saw `config hot reload applied`; a gateway started through `src/gateway/test-helpers.e2e.ts` has no recovery owner and the helper exposes no way to supply one.

**So the accurate statement is not "no observable effect". It is that the only config path this change affects is the one my harness cannot reload, and that path is the reported symptom.** Everything else an ephemeral gateway *can* hot-reload turns out to be resolved by core from the live snapshot and is genuinely unaffected by this patch, which is worth knowing on its own.

**This is cheap for a maintainer to settle.** On a managed gateway the same probe discriminates in one run: set `agents.entries.main.tools.allow` to a bogus tool, send a Feishu group message (fails with `No callable tools remain`), remove the allowlist, send another. Pre-fix the second message still fails; with this patch it recovers. I am happy to hand over the probe script, or to open it as the separate harness PR described below.

What stands independently of that: the code-level asymmetry, group turns carry the account-start config while DMs refresh, which your review has now confirmed twice with `Findings: None`, plus the dead `if (isDirect)` branch this removes at net −10 production lines. If that is not enough on its own, I would rather you say so than have me keep dressing it up.

**What I would rather not do is smuggle that harness into this PR.** The repo has no Feishu ingress test harness today, and the same gap blocks msteams, `extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler.test-helpers.ts:189-204` builds `createActivityHandler` with `onMessage: () => handler`, discarding the message callback, so plain inbound messages cannot be driven there either. A harness that fixes this is shared infrastructure serving several channels, not a detail of this one-line-plus-deletion fix, and `CONTRIBUTING.md` asks for one thing per PR.

I am happy to build it as its own PR and then link it back here as the proof for this change. If maintainers would rather have it inline, or would rather apply `proof: override` given `Findings: None` / `Security: None` and the net −10 production delta, say which and I will follow.

### Rebase and exact-head validation (2026-08-11)

Rebased onto `2cc11aff38` as requested; no conflicts, and neither changed file had been touched on main since the branch point.

**The feishu lane is already red on that main.** `pnpm test:extension feishu`:

| | total | passed | failed |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `2cc11aff38` (main, detached) | 1575 | 1547 | **28** |
| this branch rebased onto it | 1578 | 1550 | **28** |

The two failure sets are name-for-name identical (diffed), so this branch adds three passing tests and changes nothing else. Pre-existing failures include `Error: lazy additive state schema block is missing for cron_job_runtime_authorities` in `thread-bindings.test.ts` and a dedupe-replay assertion, unrelated to this change, and per `CONTRIBUTING.md` not this PR's to fix. Flagging it so the red lane is not read as caused here.

Focused file after rebase: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/feishu/src/bot.test.ts` → 103 passed, exit 0. `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` on both changed files → exit 0.

The branch went 24 commits behind again while that validation ran, so `BEHIND` is not a stable state to chase here; happy to refresh again on request or to leave it to takeover, since **Allow edits by maintainers** is enabled.

### On the flagged stored-data-model change

The review flagged `serialized state: extensions/feishu/src/bot.test.ts` and asked for migration or upgrade-compatibility proof. I believe that is a false positive: the only serialization in that file is `JSON.stringify` of in-memory fixtures, a message `content` payload and a temp config written to `os.tmpdir()` and deleted in `finally`. No schema, no SQLite, no state directory, no persisted user data, and nothing outside the test process. The production diff (`bot.ts`, −10 lines) touches no storage path at all. Happy to be corrected if the check meant something else.

---

*AI-assisted: authored with Claude. Every file and line reference above was read on `main` at `fa03d9b913`, and every test result quoted is from a local run of the stated command.*

Follow-up to #122299.

AI-assisted: this maintainer-requested cleanup used Codex-backed implementation and review.

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw still had a broad tail of locally reimplemented coercion bodies after the earlier consolidation rounds. Exact string, record, numeric, date, Boolean, CLI-argument, and error adapters were duplicated across core, plugins, packages, scripts, and UI. That made equivalent boundaries easy to drift and left ownership difficult to enforce mechanically.

This is round four of the explicitly requested coercion cleanup. It follows the semantic body scan after #122299 and consolidates only contract-exact implementations.

## Why This Change Was Made

The patch resolves 87 exact string/record candidates: 85 migrate to their existing canonical owners, while two remain local because one script is copied standalone and one trusted current-tree harness runs against an old target working directory. It also migrates 61 numeric bodies, six date adapters, the compatible Boolean and CLI grammars, canonical-name collision families, and dense exact error clusters. It adds the hostile-input-safe `toStructuredErrorObject`, keeps dependency-light script argument helpers behind a matching runtime declaration companion, and removes deprecated internal text-runtime bypasses.

The ownership guard now covers 101 explicitly allowed declarations and a small direct-export completeness audit. Its earlier structural body mini-interpreter and implementation-coupled tests were removed under Repair Doctrine; the executable declaration inventory and focused export audit are the canonical enforcement path.

Current-main overlap was preserved during rebase, including the explicit OpenAI provider selection, Telegram session-route owner, suite test-support classification, and Gateway session helper rename. No config, protocol, SQLite schema, dependency, version, release, or changelog surface changes.

## User Impact

There is no intended user-visible behavior change. Maintainers get one smaller and more enforceable coercion surface, fewer local policy copies, and canonical hostile-error handling while existing call-site semantics remain unchanged.

title: fix(ai): continue cached OpenAI WebSocket turns
body:
Closes #122482
Related: #122194

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where direct OpenAI API-key users who selected cached WebSocket transport would reuse the socket but still resend the full conversation on each warm turn. Real provider output was rejected as changed history, so `previous_response_id` continuation never activated.

## Why This Change Was Made

Continuation matching now compares JSON values independently of object insertion order while preserving normal JSON omission semantics. At the assistant replay boundary, it removes only provider delivery metadata that reconstructed history cannot contain (`id`, `status`, `output_text.annotations`, and `output_text.logprobs`) while keeping semantic fields such as role, phase, text, reasoning shape, and tool-call data fail-closed.

The direct API-key default remains SSE. This PR does not add WebSocket preconnect/prewarm or the broader SSE continuation cache proposed in #122194.

Production LOC: +31/-14 (net +17) | Tests: +43/-7 (net +36) | Docs: +2/-2 (net 0)

## User Impact

Explicit `websocket-cached` and `auto` users on the built-in OpenAI Responses runtime now get the continuation behavior those modes promise: one session socket, `previous_response_id`, and suffix-only input when history is unchanged. Semantic history or request changes still invalidate continuation and send a full request.

The provider reference now accurately documents SSE as the direct API-key default and lists all supported explicit transport modes.

## Evidence

- Pre-fix production-path regression: a realistic completed OpenAI response with citation annotations, logprobs, and provider field order caused the second request to omit `previous_response_id`; the new regression fails on the old comparator and passes with this fix.
- Focused exact-head tests: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/ai/src/transports/openai-responses-websocket.test.ts packages/ai/src/transports/openai-responses-websocket-client.test.ts` -> 2 files, 29 tests passed.
- Docs/static proof: full MDX check (770 files), docs/source formatting, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Changed-surface gate: core, coreTests, and docs passed locally after the remote Crabbox/Testbox backend was unavailable; core/test typechecks, lint, max-lines ratchet, deadcode, plugin boundaries, import cycles, schema and package guards were green.
- Exact-head pull-request CI: [run 31569182042](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/31569182042) completed successfully on `dabe607efda854be74cc70e7432e19c321f15e6c`.
- Authenticated live OpenAI A/B on the reviewed head: 48/48 complete; no WebSocket fallback, warning, or failure; cached WebSocket was the actual transport for 16/16 sequential turns; 12/12 warm turns reused the connection and continued with `previous_response_id`.
- Warm sequential medians: first provider event 135.839 ms cached WebSocket vs 333 ms SSE; total duration 1082.076 ms vs 1109.844 ms; TTFT was comparable at 963.535 ms vs 920.231 ms, so this is a correctness/warm-start repair rather than a claim that WebSocket is universally faster.
- Final Codex autoreview: clean; TruffleHog clean; patch correct 0.98.
- Dependency contract review: latest sibling Codex typed continuation/suffix logic plus installed OpenAI SDK Responses WebSocket serialization and output types were inspected directly.

title: refactor(discord): split voice lifecycle ownership
body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes Discord voice races where leaving during a pending join could reconnect later, a stopped session could subscribe after authorization, decoded STT work could outlive leave, followed-user state could resurrect an older move, realtime connect could report ready after close, and provider-reset completions could leak into a newer voice generation.

The previous voice implementation also concentrated connection, follow, receive, realtime, playback, turn, and consult ownership in two files over 4,000 lines, making these lifecycle invariants difficult to express and verify.

## Why This Change Was Made

The voice subsystem is split by lifecycle owner into runtime, guild session, following, receive, realtime session, playback, turns, and consult modules. One per-guild generation now authorizes connection publication, capture, realtime state, transcripts, and playback; provider continuity retains its own epoch. Playback and exact-speech state are closed unions rather than parallel booleans.

Discord startup keeps its existing outer lazy boundary, while STT/TTS no longer loads realtime provider and consult machinery: `voice-session.ts` dynamically imports `realtime-session.runtime.ts` only for agent-proxy and bidi modes. Generic policy text and the exact-speech scraper remain byte-identical and are explicitly marked for a separate owner-reviewed realtime-voice follow-up.

## User Impact

Discord voice leave, follow, capture, and realtime operations are last-event-wins. Stale async work can no longer reconnect, subscribe, transcribe, play, publish readiness, or deliver provider completions after its voice generation has closed.

There is no configuration or Plugin SDK change. Existing voice instructions, consult/control tool schemas, transcript-source behavior, and STT/TTS behavior are preserved.

## Evidence

Regression provenance and before/after proof:

- All six new order-sensitive regressions were run against the mechanical split commit and failed for the intended reason: pending leave (leave returned false), late receiver subscription, post-leave STT execution, stale followed-user publication, ready-after-close, and stale provider transcript delivery.
- The same six tests pass after the lifecycle-authority commit.
- Exact source comparison against pre-split `realtime.ts` confirms the assembled instruction builder and consult/control tool assembly are byte-identical.

Validation on head `4119d4a90a416efa0ed2e2d70d62fc4849f88875`:

- Focused lifecycle/follow/receive batch: 3 files, 100 tests passed.
- Focused playback/turns/consults batch: 3 files, 76 tests passed.
- Runtime composition E2E: join → audio ingress → agent dispatch → playback → leave passed.
- Full Discord batch: 220 files, 2,754 tests passed.
- Extension package boundary compile: 124 plugins passed.
- `node scripts/check-changed.mjs --base <frozen-merge-base>`: green, including dead-code scans, production/test typechecks, extension lint, database-first guard, and zero runtime import cycles.
- `pnpm build`: green; no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warning.
- `pnpm lint:tmp:export-name-collisions`: green.
- `pnpm check:wrapper-shadowing`: green.

## What Problem This Solves

Unsupported local documents (DOCX, XLSX, …) currently yield a capability marker and dead-end even when the host-run agent can inspect the saved file itself.

## Why This Change Was Made

`unsupported-format` now retains the cache-approved local path through preprocessing, then promotes the plain marker only after the final embedded provider, owner, tool, sandbox, and filesystem policy permit host reads. The marker directs the agent to extract the file itself; OOXML gets an unzip hint. URL-only attachments, generic ACP, sandboxed sessions, unsafe filenames, and operator-policy rejections retain the plain marker. No parsers, dependencies, or config.

## User Impact

A default host-run agent can inspect a locally saved unsupported document instead of asking the sender to paste its contents.

## Maintainer Decision

Approved by Ayaan on 2026-08-12: eligible embedded host runs may include the root-approved absolute attachment path in model context after sandbox, filesystem-scope, final provider/tool-policy, and authoritative owner gates pass.

title: fix(agents): scope quota failures to auth profiles
body:
## Summary

### High Level TLDR

A quota failure on one auth profile could pause the shared command lane for 30 minutes, blocking unrelated sessions and providers before they reached a model. A user-selected auth profile also collapsed same-provider auth routing to one candidate, so a second configured account was never tried.

This removes provider-failure control from command-lane capacity and makes a user auth pin a durable first preference instead of a strict singleton. Only the failed profile enters cooldown; eligible same-provider profiles remain available. Explicit provider/model selection stays strict.

- keep quota/manual/circuit suspension markers for diagnostics and recovery, without changing lane concurrency
- try a valid user-pinned profile first, then ordered same-provider profiles
- skip only a cooled/disabled profile and return to the persisted pin after recovery
- preserve strict provider bindings and explicit provider/model selection
- include compatible external-CLI credential sources when discovering sibling profiles
- keep shutdown fencing for late suspension-marker writes

## What Problem This Solves

A failure on one provider credential must not pause unrelated work or suppress other authorized credentials for that provider. Before this change, one terminal quota failure could set a shared command lane to zero for 30 minutes, while a user-sourced auth override prevented the runner from trying a configured sibling profile.

## Evidence

- Redacted live evidence showed one OpenAI quota failure setting the shared `main` lane to zero while an unrelated provider session waited before model invocation.
- Exact-head queue integration proves a suspension marker leaves unrelated `main`-lane work runnable.
- Exact-head runner E2E proves a user-pinned profile rotates to a same-provider backup in both OpenClaw and Codex harness paths, then surfaces failure only after all eligible profiles fail.
- Exact-head results: 314 focused tests and 47 runner E2Es passed; benchmark results are recorded below.

## Root Cause

### Before behavior

1. `suspendSession` accepted a command-lane id, called `setCommandLaneConcurrency(lane, 0)`, and scheduled a default 30-minute resume timer.
2. Ordinary agent turns from different sessions and providers share the `main` lane. One terminal provider failure therefore blocked unrelated work at queue admission, before provider/model routing.
3. Runtime auth planning encoded a user-selected profile as required `user-lock` ownership. That produced one physical auth attempt and bypassed normal same-provider cooldown admission, even when another authorized profile existed.
4. External-CLI discovery also narrowed a user pin to one credential source before the planner could see ordered siblings.

The earlier repair in #93789 correctly deferred lane suspension while model fallback candidates remained, but terminal/direct failures could still lock a shared lane. The remaining invariant violation was architectural: provider/profile availability was controlling a process-wide scheduling primitive.

The Codex dependency contract confirms that one app-server client has one active `auth_manager`/account and surfaces usage-limit reset metadata. Cross-account selection is therefore OpenClaw's responsibility at its prepared profile/client boundary, not something one Codex client performs internally:

- https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/2f108f9fd970ed73df7e984d3a661acc02f33abc/codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/account_processor.rs#L818-L839
- https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/2f108f9fd970ed73df7e984d3a661acc02f33abc/codex-rs/protocol/src/error.rs#L449-L550

### RCA evidence

A redacted production incident reproduced the complete ordering:

- one OpenAI subscription profile returned a usage-limit error
- the exact profile received cooldown/reset metadata
- the terminal suspension path set the shared `main` lane to concurrency zero
- a separate session using an unrelated provider remained queued before any model call
- a second configured OpenAI profile was not attempted because the session auth override was user-sourced

The deployed base, active overlay patches, and persisted runtime state were inspected separately. No overlay touched the causal lane-suspension/profile-planning ownership paths.

## Real behavior proof

Closest feasible environment: exact-head runner E2E with the real auth planner/controller and mocked provider transport, plus the real process command queue.

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
    src/agents/model-fallback.run-embedded.e2e.test.ts \
    src/agents/embedded-agent-runner.run-embedded-agent.auth-profile-rotation.e2e.test.ts

OpenClaw 2026.8.1 (82342d0)
Test Files  2 passed (2)
Tests       47 passed (47)
```

The E2E matrix proves:

- a rate-limited user pin rotates to the next same-provider profile
- the failed pin receives cooldown while the sibling succeeds
- a cooled pin is skipped on the next turn without replacing the persisted preference
- Codex-harness retry changes from the user-pinned OpenAI profile to the backup OpenAI profile and attributes the backup as automatic
- only after all same-provider profiles fail does the terminal failure surface

The queue integration proves an OpenAI suspension marker does not block unrelated `main`-lane work.

Performance benchmark: Node 25.9.0, same host/workload, 3 warmups plus 30 measured samples, using a 10 ms suspension TTL to measure unrelated `main`-lane admission.

```text
baseline ce53f7e82e2: median 10.181346 ms, p95 10.536215 ms
final    82342d00b00: median  0.012239 ms, p95  0.044799 ms
```

This measures removal of the artificial queue wait; it is not a provider latency benchmark.

## What was not tested

- The patched branch was not deployed to the production Gateway, and no real account was deliberately driven into quota exhaustion.
- Blacksmith Testbox validation was unavailable because its authentication had expired; AWS Crabbox was unavailable because the broker was not logged in.
- A full changed-file gate could not be cleanly reproduced in the linked worktree because its borrowed dependency tree carried unrelated terminal-core and generated Plugin SDK baseline failures. Exact-head focused suites and the E2E build passed.

## Verification

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
    src/agents/session-suspension.test.ts \
    src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/failure-suspension.test.ts \
    src/agents/model-fallback.probe.test.ts \
    src/agents/model-fallback.test.ts \
    src/agents/runtime-plan/prepare-auth.test.ts \
    src/agents/auth-profiles/external-cli-auth-selection.test.ts \
    src/gateway/server-close.test.ts \
    src/gateway/server-lanes.test.ts \
    src/gateway/server-lanes.hook-group.test.ts

Test Files  9 passed (9)
Tests       314 passed (314)
```

- structured autoreview: clean, no accepted/actionable findings
- dependency secret scan: clean
- production LOC: `+116 -373` (net `-257`)
- test LOC: `+357 -653` (net `-296`)
- docs LOC: `+4 -3` (net `+1`)

The production reduction comes from deleting lane suspension/resume timers, gateway suspended-lane publication policy, and their duplicate lifecycle machinery. No config, environment variable, protocol, or SQLite schema surface is added.


## Current-head live proof — 2026-08-09

Exact PR head `1f1daa0ac079e4ec91fc0ee2b3c494c016dba4c5` was applied to the managed production Gateway aggregate on base `c3a0d3e58ad599343b12c175d03aef909cdff83b`. The updater reported this PR and all five other configured open overlays as applied. Exact aggregate source hash: `62ca757d0c2f79549e0a11bf19dcc021b86d838351521b1b049e9467178e25d1`.

Redacted precondition, queried after deployment and before either model turn:

```json
{
  "openaiProfileCount": 2,
  "openaiCooldownCount": 1
}
```

No cooldown was cleared and no profile pin was changed.

Unrelated-provider command:

```console
$ openclaw agent exec --model ollama-cloud/glm-5.2 --no-auth-env-only --code-mode direct --timeout 180 --json "Reply exactly GLM_PROFILE_SCOPE_OK and nothing else."
```

Observed result:

```json

  "ok": true,
  "status": "ok",
  "final": "GLM_PROFILE_SCOPE_OK",
  "model": "glm-5.2",
  "provider": "ollama-cloud"
}
```

Eligible same-provider sibling command:

```console
$ openclaw agent exec --model openai/gpt-5.6-sol --no-auth-env-only --code-mode direct --timeout 180 --json "Reply exactly OPENAI_PROFILE_SCOPE_OK and nothing else."
```

Observed result:

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "status": "ok",
  "final": "OPENAI_PROFILE_SCOPE_OK",
  "model": "gpt-5.6-sol",
  "provider": "openai"

```

Post-run bookkeeping recorded success for one redacted OpenAI profile while the other profile remained in its persisted quota cooldown. The unrelated provider also completed, proving that the auth-profile suspension did not pause the shared command lane or suppress another provider.

Compatibility decision: an explicit auth pin remains the first preference, but a quota-blocked pinned profile does not suppress another authorized profile for the same provider. This is deliberate so one exhausted credential cannot wedge that agent across providers.

The upstream Codex app-server contract is account-specific: `codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/account_processor.rs` accepts external auth updates for an explicit account and emits the previous-account hint used to refresh the correct workspace; `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/schema/json/ChatgptAuthTokensRefreshParams.json` carries that account-specific refresh input. The OpenClaw fix keeps the cooldown at the corresponding auth-profile boundary.

Final runtime state: Gateway RPC and verbose health `ok: true`; Telegram connected; service restarts `0`. Private profile labels, account data, chat/session identifiers, host details, and process identifiers are omitted.

title: fix(codex): preserve allowed tools under channel policy
body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes two related regressions in Codex channel runs with explicit tool policy:

1. Any non-empty deny list marked the entire Codex native tool surface restricted. A channel or agent policy such as `deny: ["tts", "music_generate"]` therefore disabled unrelated native tools including plan, shell, file, image, and collaboration tools even though none was denied.
2. When a policy genuinely must isolate Codex native tools, the policy-filtered OpenClaw `update_plan` replacement was deferred and successful calls were not projected as structured plan events, so channel progress lost its live checklist.

The over-broad isolation started in `409fb7abcaceb2ab2f2b584d393dd38fedb74ac5` when explicit channel policy began disabling the whole native Codex surface.

## What Changed

- Added optional harness metadata, `conversationToolPolicySafeDenyTools`, declaring exact known OpenClaw denies that are fully enforced outside the harness-native surface.
- Native tools remain enabled only when every expanded deny is both a known core tool and present in that audited safe list.
- Finite allowlists, undeclared known tools, unknown names, wildcards, and groups containing any undeclared name still isolate the complete native surface.
- The Codex safe list is positive and conservative. It includes OpenClaw-only capabilities such as `tts` and `music_generate`; omissions and future tools fail closed.
- For runs that still require native isolation, the OpenClaw `update_plan` replacement remains directly model-visible and successful calls reuse the structured plan projector.

## Review Hardening

The first revision declared native overlaps. ClawSweeper correctly identified that an omitted overlap could fail open. This revision inverts the contract: a harness declares only deny names proven safe to exempt. An omitted or mistakenly unknown name now isolates the native surface, so catalog growth cannot silently weaken policy enforcement.

## Security Properties

- Denied OpenClaw tools are never added back to the catalog.
- Only exact, known, audited safe denies preserve harness-native tools.
- Finite allowlists remain restrictive.
- Undeclared known tools, native overlaps, unknown names, wildcards, and mixed groups remain restrictive.
- Even a harness that lists an unknown name cannot exempt it because core also requires `isKnownCoreToolId`.
- Third-party harnesses that omit the new metadata retain the previous conservative behavior.

## Codex Dependency Contract Checked

The bundled dependency is `@openai/codex` 0.147.0. I inspected the matching `rust-v0.147.0` source at `be6e8eac029b183056b7e4402879f15d2c85f61b`:

- `codex-rs/core/src/tools/spec_plan.rs:848-851` assembles shell, MCP-resource, utility, and collaboration sources into one registry.
- `codex-rs/core/src/tools/spec_plan.rs:875-1040` registers the native shell, plan, request-input, apply-patch, and image capabilities.
- `codex-rs/core/src/tools/spec_plan.rs:1043-1131` registers native collaboration capabilities.
- `codex-rs/core/src/tools/hosted_spec.rs:14-45` defines the hosted web-search surface.
- `codex-rs/config/src/mcp_types.rs:209-215` and `codex-rs/config/src/types.rs:853-879` expose per-tool filtering for MCP servers/plugins, not a global arbitrary native-tool deny surface.

Therefore OpenClaw must retain full native isolation whenever a policy might overlap Codex-native or unknown capabilities. The positive safe-deny declaration is the fail-closed owner boundary for exact OpenClaw-only denies.

## Regression Proof

The new core regression failed before the resolver change: `deny: ["tts", "music_generate"]` produced `pluginHarnessToolPolicyRestricted: true`. It now verifies:

- audited exact denies (`tts`, `music_generate`) do not isolate Codex native tools;
- an undeclared known deny still isolates;
- a declared-but-unknown name still isolates;
- native overlaps, groups, wildcard denies, and finite allowlists still isolate;
- the existing restricted-run coverage proves `update_plan` remains direct and emits a normalized structured plan event when native isolation is required.

## Evidence

Exact rebased head: `6a77a0414f7`

- Core harness selection: 224/224 passed across both core configurations.
- Codex harness and run-attempt suites: 160/160 passed.
- Core and extension production TypeScript: passed on the exact head.
- Core and extension test TypeScript: passed during the review-fix validation cycle.
- Plugin SDK baseline generation, drift, exports, and surface checks: passed.
- Formatting, targeted core/extension lint, dependency pins, patch guards, dead exports, database/state, runtime-sidecar, import-cycle, webhook, and pairing guards: passed.
- `check:changed` advanced through its in-scope checks but current `origin/main` independently fails `plugins:boundary-report:ci` because `plugin-sdk-media-understanding-public-demotion` is overdue. The same failure reproduces without this PR; remaining underlying checks were run directly and passed.

## Remaining Owner Verification

- A maintainer still needs to approve the public optional harness metadata contract.
- This update does not claim a post-branch live Telegram/app-server deployment run; that runtime proof remains to be attached from an environment running this branch.


## Final-Head Telegram Proof

Exact head: `fc3473b2b09`

Command shape (secrets and local paths omitted): `run-mock-sut-user-e2e.mjs --backend claude-cli --dm --record ... --output ...` with `channels.telegram.direct["*"].tools.deny = ["tts", "music_generate"]` and the Codex app-server harness selected.

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where the shared `checks-ui` worker could fail unrelated Control UI changes when a predecessor suite cached the real clipboard module, a lazy update dialog retained module state across jsdom suites, or a delayed tooltip callback ran after Vitest replaced the browser realm.

The task-suggestion regression drives the actual Clipboard API and fallback owners instead of asserting a later mock export that production may not reference. Tooltip trigger detection now uses the HTML namespace rather than the transient global `HTMLElement`, which is also correct for HTML nodes created by another document realm.

This is the owner-boundary fix: it preserves the production clipboard error path and update-confirmation behavior, while removing test-order coupling instead of adding waits or weakening assertions.

No user-facing workflow changes. Maintainers get deterministic Control UI CI, and tooltip triggers remain correct across document realms.

- Exact local `checks-ui` packing emitted `ReferenceError: HTMLElement is not defined` from a delayed tooltip slot callback after jsdom teardown.
- The new cross-document tooltip regression failed before the owner fix with `expected null to be truthy`.

title: fix(slack): scope enterprise channel and user policies by workspace
body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Enterprise Grid org installs could apply a Slack channel, user, or bot policy to the wrong workspace when two workspaces reused the same Slack-local ID.

## Why This Change Was Made

Slack's trusted per-event workspace ID is now part of channel and sender policy identity. For Enterprise Grid events, only `team:<team-id>:channel:<channel-id>` and `team:<team-id>:user:<actor-id>` entries are eligible; bare channel, user, and bot IDs do not match. The `*` wildcard remains global. Standard workspace installs retain bare-ID compatibility.

Qualified actor selectors accept Slack member IDs (`U...` and `W...`) and bot IDs (`B...`) because bot messages use `bot_id` as the sender identity.

Enterprise configuration validation enforces the same contract at startup, so unsafe bare channel and actor policies fail visibly instead of becoming cross-workspace policy.

## User Impact

Enterprise Grid operators must qualify concrete Slack channel and actor policy entries with the workspace team ID. Events from one workspace cannot inherit a policy written for another workspace merely because the Slack-local ID is the same.

## Evidence

- Added direct regressions proving Enterprise events reject bare channel and actor policy IDs and accept only matching workspace-qualified entries.
- Added parser, validator, and matching coverage for workspace-qualified Slack bot IDs.
- Preserved bare-ID behavior for standard workspace installs and wildcard behavior for both installation types.
- Passed 459 focused Slack tests across 13 policy and runtime test files.
- Targeted formatting and direct Slack lint pass.
- Existing live Slack checks on this branch used workspace-qualified channel and user entries for both an Enterprise Grid org install and a standard workspace install; unrelated actors were ignored.
